title: German Center for Mental Health (DZPG): “Mechanism-Based, Modular Psychotherapy for Traumatized Adolescents and Young Adults: A Confirmatory Study”
summary:
The present study builds on the preceding feasibility study of Mechanism-Based, Modular Psychotherapy (MeMoPsy), which primarily investigated the feasibility and acceptability of the MeMoPsy treatment and gathered initial evidence on the extent to which MeMoPsy contributes to symptom reduction (DRKS00034058) (Seitz et al. 2025). The present study will now investigate the efficacy of MeMoPsy compared with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for young people aged 15 to 25 years with mental health disorders and adverse childhood experiences.
Traumatic experiences in childhood, such as abuse or neglect, substantially increase the risk of developing mental health disorders later in life. Affected individuals often experience more severe courses of illness, and conventional psychotherapies tend to be less effective for them. This may be because standard therapies are primarily designed around individual diagnoses and often do not sufficiently take into account the individually varying consequences of adverse childhood experiences. According to the current evidence, the following three mechanisms mediate the association between adverse childhood experiences and later mental health disorders: (1) increased sensitivity to rejection, (2) difficulties regulating emotions and arousal, and (3) problems in interpersonal relationships. Identifying and treating these mechanisms is the aim of the MeMoPsy treatment. MeMoPsy uses so-called “modules,” which comprise different therapeutic interventions tailored to these three mechanisms and the consequences of adverse childhood experiences. Instead of providing a uniform diagnosis-specific treatment ("one-fits-all approach"), the modular approach offers the opportunity to combine modules in a targeted manner in order to address precisely the difficulties or mechanisms from which an individual person suffers. For example, treatment for a patient experiencing difficulties regulating emotions and arousal would include the module specifically designed to support the management of emotions and arousal. Initial evidence for the effectiveness of modular therapy was provided by the MoBa study (Schramm et al. 2024), which demonstrated favorable treatment outcomes and high satisfaction with the modular approach.
Building on the MoBa study, MeMoPsy consists of a core component focusing on establishing a therapeutic relationship and trauma processing, as well as up to three additional modules targeting changes in the specific mechanisms. The selection of the additional modules is determined by an allocation-algorithm based on self-report questionnaires. The MeMoPsy feasibility study (DRKS00034058) successfully demonstrated the applicability of the approach in routine clinical practice. With the involvement of two experts with lived experience (Patient and Public Involvement, PPI), an innovative, personalized psychotherapeutic approach was developed for young people with mental health disorders and adverse childhood experiences in an outpatient treatment setting. The overarching aim of the feasibility study was to investigate the acceptability, feasibility, and symptom changes associated with this Mechanism-Based, Modular Psychotherapy (MeMoPsy) compared with standard Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), a widely used and effective form of psychotherapy. Since May 2024, the feasibility study has been conducted at three sites in Germany (Heidelberg, Mannheim, and Berlin). The final assessment is expected to take place in November 2026. Between May 2024 and December 2025, all planned N = 80 patients aged between 15 and 26 years were enrolled in the feasibility study; n = 5 had to be excluded. Psychometric data are available for 77% of participants at mid-treatment and for 81% at the end of treatment. Initial preliminary analyses of data collected before treatment indicate a sample suffering from high psychological distress with a range of mental disorders and pronounced childhood experiences of abuse and neglect. Initial qualitative interviews suggest that these highly distressed patients experience MeMoPsy’s structured and goal-oriented therapeutic approach as helpful. The early treatment dropouts that can already be evaluated were n = 4 in the MeMoPsy group and n = 7 in the CBT group (as of October 2026).
A large new study will now investigate the efficacy of MeMoPsy in a scientifically rigorous manner. A total of 250 adolescents and young adults aged 15 to 25 years from Heidelberg, Mannheim, Berlin, and Ulm will participate; the participating institutions collaborate within the German Center for Mental Health. Participants will be randomly allocated to two groups: one group will receive MeMoPsy, while the other will receive standard Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), as typically provided within the German healthcare system. At the end of treatment, the two therapies will be compared to determine which treatment was more effective in reducing mental health symptoms. The study will also examine whether the mechanisms described above change over the course of treatment. Changes between the beginning and end of therapy will be assessed using questionnaires, interviews, smartphone-based assessments, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and saliva samples, which will be used to assess cortisol levels as a measure of stress. Overall, the study aims to determine whether this tailored MeMoPsy approach can help young people with adverse childhood experiences more effectively than existing standard treatments.
conditions: Mental disorders according to DSM-5, assessed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Disorders – Clinician Version (SCID-5-CV, Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019a) and the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Personality Disorders (SCID-5-PD, Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019b, subchapter Borderline Personality Disorder).  In addition to a mental disorder, participants must have experienced moderate to severe adverse childhood experiences (Häuser et al., 2011), as assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (Klinitzke et al., 2011).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-	Capacity to provide informed consent
-	Meets criteria for one or more mental disorders according to DSM-5 at T-1, assessed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Disorders – Clinician Version (SCID-5-CV; Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019a) or the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Personality Disorders (SCID-5-PD; Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019b). At T-2 (screening), participants must score above the cut-off on at least one of the module-specific questionnaires: RSQ (Module 1 cut-off: ≥13.459.88); DERS-16 (Module 2 cut-off: ≥56.2246.97); or the EB-45, “Interpersonal Relations” (IR) subscale (Module 3 cut-off: ≥17.6713).
-	At T-2, scores in at least one of the five subscales of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) must fall within the “moderate to severe” range, with severity classification based on Häuser et al. (2011).
-	Fluent German language proficiency
-	Valid statutory health insurance coverage
Exclusion criteria:
-	Currently meets criteria for one or more mental disorders requiring alternative, diagnosis-specific treatment, assessed using the SCID-5-CV or the AQ-10 (Autism Spectrum Disorder screening):
•	moderate to severe substance use disorder (exception: 3 months of abstinence and an intention to remain abstinent throughout treatment)
•	severe autism spectrum disorder that interferes with participation in regular therapy sessions, based on an individual clinical assessment supported by the AQ-10
•	acute psychotic symptoms
•	acute manic symptoms
-	Concurrent psychotherapy
-	Residence more than 70 km from any of the study sites
-	Severe cognitive impairment, assessed using the mini-q (IQ < 70)
-	Inability or unwillingness to abstain from substance use during therapy sessions, based on an individual clinical assessment
-	Acute suicidality, assessed using the SCID-5-CV and based on an individual clinical assessment
-	History of a severe illness that interferes with participation in regular therapy sessions, based on an individual clinical assessment
-	Change in current psychotropic medication or initiation of new psychotropic medication within the two weeks prior to study enrollment (at least 3 weeks for fluoxetine)
-	Participation in the MeMoPsy feasibility study

Exclusion criteria for the optional MRI assessment at the Heidelberg and Mannheim sites:
-	Pacemaker or other medical devices implanted in or attached to the body
-	Metal implants or metallic foreign bodies in or on the body
-	(Potential) pregnancy
-	In cases of noise hypersensitivity, ear damage, or claustrophobia, participation in the MRI assessment is discouraged.
